1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Multi-turn dialogue is central to how large language models are deployed, yet a persistent failure accompanies even the most fluent generation: as conversations grow longer, models pay progressively less attention to the system-prompt goals that define their task. \citet{dongre2026attention} measured 27--48\% Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR) decline across 12 models over 50 turns, even as residual stream probes confirm that goal representations persist (AUC\,=\,0.98). This is not just a measurement artifact---exploratory evaluation suggests it can degrade instruction compliance by up to 24 percentage points on content-constrained tasks (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
4	
5	Existing remedies address this decay at inference time. Split-softmax \citep{li2024measuring} separates instruction from conversation tokens; StreamingLLM \citep{xiao2024streaming} retains anchor tokens; Gated Attention \citep{qiu2025gated} applies per-head sigmoid gates within a single forward pass. None of these intervenes during training. A natural alternative is to optimize goal attention directly through auxiliary attention losses trained alongside next-token prediction (NTP). Yet this strategy rests on an untested assumption: that attention patterns learned under teacher forcing transfer to autoregressive generation. Classical exposure bias research \citep{bengio2015scheduled,lamb2016professor} has shown that teacher forcing creates a training--inference mismatch for RNN sequence models, but whether this mismatch extends to auxiliary attention objectives in multi-turn transformers remains unknown.
6	
7	We test this assumption. We introduce ThreadGate, per-layer content-and-turn-conditioned gates on the residual stream ($x_{l+1} = x_l + g_l \cdot f_l(x_l)$), designed not as a solution but as a controlled testbed for isolating failure mechanisms. A five-way comparison (ThreadGate, +PCGrad, Uniform Gate, LoRA-only, Base) forms a causal exclusion chain (\S\ref{sec:comparison-design}): each adjacent pair rules out one alternative hypothesis---turn conditioning, gating mechanism, gradient conflict---tracing the failure to its root cause.
8

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\looseness=-1 The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP self-recovers because the task (predict one token from a prefix) is identical at training and inference \citep{he2019exposure}; GAR optimizes a \emph{global property of the prefix}---attention allocation to goal tokens---that has no autoregressive counterpart. Per-head analysis confirms this selectivity: heads with higher TF GAR shift most under AR generation ($r$\,=\,0.743; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-kl}). Any auxiliary attention objective paired with teacher forcing should face the same barrier when targeting distributional properties rather than the prediction itself.

\paragraph{Why NTP self-recovers but GAR does not.} NTP self-recovers because prediction is the same task at both regimes; exposure bias shifts the \emph{input distribution} but not the \emph{loss function}. GAR optimizes a global property of attention flow through layers \citep{abnar2020quantifying} over model-generated tokens that has no training-time analogue, explaining why the TF--AR gap is order-of-magnitude for GAR-ours but negligible for NTP. Crucially, the collapse is selective: GAR-ours (last-token attention) collapses 8--27$\times$ while GAR-Dongre (all-token attention) shows negligible shift (${\leq}$1.3$\times$). This asymmetry implies that the training-time GAR signal concentrates attention at a specific position (last token of each turn), a pattern that is brittle under distribution shift; the diffuse attention measured by GAR-Dongre is robust precisely because it was never specifically optimized.

\paragraph{Alternative explanations.} Our causal exclusion identifies exposure bias as the primary contributing factor consistent with all evidence, but we cannot rule out all alternatives. KV cache drift---the progressive corruption of cached key-value representations as model-generated tokens replace ground-truth tokens---could compound exposure bias or operate independently. Disentangling the two would require interventions that selectively reset KV cache states at turn boundaries, which we leave to future work. The PCGrad exclusion rules out gradient \emph{direction} conflict but not magnitude imbalance: NTP magnitude dominance grows from 7.5$\times$ to 14.7$\times$ across epochs (25.7$\times$ on Llama), meaning the GAR gradient is effectively suppressed even when not conflicting. Whether magnitude rebalancing (e.g., GradNorm; \citealp{chen2018gradnorm}) would improve AR transfer remains untested.

\paragraph{Downstream effects.} Instruction retention ($\beta$\,=\,3) shows late-turn compliance rising from 75.9\% to 87.0\% (+11.1\,pp, $p$\,=\,0.077; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}). Content constraints benefit most (+23.8\,pp), consistent with GAR targeting cross-turn semantic coherence rather than locally-verifiable procedural rules. However, the overall correlation between GAR-ours and instruction retention is weak ($r$\,=\,0.200, $p$\,=\,0.007; $r^2$\,=\,0.04), reinforcing the interpretation of GAR as a diagnostic probe rather than a direct optimization target: high TF GAR is a necessary signal that the loss is working but not a sufficient predictor of downstream compliance.

\paragraph{SS and steering as substitutes.} \looseness=-1 SS provides training-time mitigation with no inference cost; steering provides inference-time recovery with PPL cost. At $\beta$\,=\,5 the two converge (SS GAR\,=\,0.717 vs.\ TG\,=\,0.727). SS is preferable when inference budgets are tight, steering when retraining is infeasible.

2	
3	Multi-turn dialogue is central to how large language models are deployed, yet a persistent failure accompanies even the most fluent generation: as conversations grow longer, models pay progressively less attention to the system-prompt goals that define their task. \citet{dongre2026attention} measured 27--48\% Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR) decline across 12 models over 50 turns, even as residual stream probes confirm that goal representations persist (AUC\,=\,0.98). 4	
5	Existing remedies address this decay at inference time. Split-softmax \citep{li2024measuring} separates instruction from conversation tokens; StreamingLLM \citep{xiao2024streaming} retains anchor tokens; Gated Attention \citep{qiu2025gated} applies per-head sigmoid gates within a single forward pass. NTP self-recovers because the task (predict one token from a prefix) is identical at training and inference \citep{he2019exposure}; GAR optimizes a \emph{global property of the prefix}---attention allocation to goal tokens---that has no autoregressive counterpart. Per-head analysis confirms this selectivity: heads with higher TF GAR shift most under AR generation ($r$\,=\,0.743; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-kl}). Any auxiliary attention objective paired with teacher forcing should face the same barrier when targeting distributional properties rather than the prediction itself.

+\looseness=-1 The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP self-recovers because prediction is the same task at both regimes \citep{he2019exposure}; GAR optimizes a \emph{global property}---attention allocation to goal tokens---that has no autoregressive counterpart. The collapse is selective: GAR-ours (last-token) collapses 8--27$\times$ while GAR-Dongre (all-token) shows negligible shift (${\leq}$1.3$\times$), implying the concentrated attention pattern is brittle under distribution shift. Per-head analysis confirms: heads with higher TF GAR shift most under AR generation ($r$\,=\,0.743; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-kl}). Any auxiliary attention objective paired with teacher forcing should face the same barrier when targeting distributional properties rather than the prediction itself.

-\paragraph{Why NTP self-recovers but GAR does not.} NTP self-recovers because prediction is the same task at both regimes; exposure bias shifts the \emph{input distribution} but not the \emph{loss function}. GAR optimizes a global property of attention flow through layers \citep{abnar2020quantifying} over model-generated tokens that has no training-time analogue, explaining why the TF--AR gap is order-of-magnitude for GAR-ours but negligible for NTP. Crucially, the collapse is selective: GAR-ours (last-token attention) collapses 8--27$\times$ while GAR-Dongre (all-token attention) shows negligible shift (${\leq}$1.3$\times$). This asymmetry implies that the training-time GAR signal concentrates attention at a specific position (last token of each turn), a pattern that is brittle under distribution shift; the diffuse attention measured by GAR-Dongre is robust precisely because it was never specifically optimized.

+\paragraph{Alternative explanations.} Our exclusion identifies exposure bias as the primary contributing factor, but KV cache drift---progressive corruption of cached representations as model-generated tokens replace ground-truth---could compound or operate independently and remains untested. The PCGrad exclusion rules out gradient \emph{direction} conflict but not magnitude imbalance (NTP dominance 7.5--14.7$\times$, 25.7$\times$ on Llama; \citealp{chen2018gradnorm}).

-\paragraph{Alternative explanations.} Our causal exclusion identifies exposure bias as the primary contributing factor consistent with all evidence, but we cannot rule out all alternatives. KV cache drift---the progressive corruption of cached key-value representations as model-generated tokens replace ground-truth tokens---could compound exposure bias or operate independently. Disentangling the two would require interventions that selectively reset KV cache states at turn boundaries, which we leave to future work. The PCGrad exclusion rules out gradient \emph{direction} conflict but not magnitude imbalance: NTP magnitude dominance grows from 7.5$\times$ to 14.7$\times$ across epochs (25.7$\times$ on Llama), meaning the GAR gradient is effectively suppressed even when not conflicting. Whether magnitude rebalancing (e.g., GradNorm; \citealp{chen2018gradnorm}) would improve AR transfer remains untested.

+\paragraph{Downstream effects.} Steering ($\beta$\,=\,3) raises late-turn compliance by +11.1\,pp ($p$\,=\,0.077), with content constraints benefiting most (+23.8\,pp; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}). The overall GAR--compliance correlation is weak ($r$\,=\,0.200, $r^2$\,=\,0.04), reinforcing GAR's role as a diagnostic probe rather than a direct optimization target.

-\paragraph{Downstream effects.} Instruction retention ($\beta$\,=\,3) shows late-turn compliance rising from 75.9\% to 87.0\% (+11.1\,pp, $p$\,=\,0.077; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-ir}). Content constraints benefit most (+23.8\,pp), consistent with GAR targeting cross-turn semantic coherence rather than locally-verifiable procedural rules. However, the overall correlation between GAR-ours and instruction retention is weak ($r$\,=\,0.200, $p$\,=\,0.007; $r^2$\,=\,0.04), reinforcing the interpretation of GAR as a diagnostic probe rather than a direct optimization target: high TF GAR is a necessary signal that the loss is working but not a sufficient predictor of downstream compliance.

\paragraph{SS and steering as substitutes.} \looseness=-1 SS provides training-time mitigation with no inference cost; steering provides inference-time recovery with PPL cost. At $\beta$\,=\,5 the two converge (SS GAR\,=\,0.717 vs.\ TG\,=\,0.727). SS is preferable when inference budgets are tight, steering when retraining is infeasible.

The result is clear: training succeeds but inference fails. All variants converge to TF GAR\,=\,0.50, yet under autoregressive generation GAR collapses to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap on Qwen-2.5-7B and 27$\times$ on Llama-3.1-8B (Figure~\ref{fig:headline}). The causal exclusion chain identifies exposure bias as the primary contributing factor consistent with all evidence: PCGrad removes gradient conflict yet \emph{worsens} AR GAR ($p$\,=\,0.002), ruling it out by \emph{modus tollens}; gating provides no benefit over LoRA-only. Crucially, inference-time steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR to 0.727, confirming that the collapse reflects attention misallocation rather than representation degradation. Scheduled sampling compresses the TF--AR gap to ${\sim}$1.3$\times$ on Qwen and ${\sim}$2.9$\times$ on Llama with no perplexity cost---the first application of scheduled sampling to auxiliary attention objectives in multi-turn transformers.

Our contributions: (1)~the first empirical characterization of exposure bias on auxiliary attention losses (8--27$\times$ TF--AR gap across two architectures); (2)~a five-way diagnostic testbed informed by seven loss design iterations, enabling causal exclusion of gradient conflict via PCGrad ($p$\,=\,0.002, effect reverses); (3)~inference-time $\beta$-steering recovers GAR to 0.727, confirming attention misallocation as the proximal cause; (4)~cross-architecture validation on Llama-3.1-8B and cross-scale validation on Qwen-2.5-1.5B; (5)~scheduled sampling compresses the TF--AR gap from 8--27$\times$ to 1.3--2.9$\times$ ($0.401\pm0.047$, three seeds on Qwen), the first transfer to auxiliary attention objectives in multi-turn transformers. Code and data are available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/turn-residual-gating}.

\subsection{Scheduled Sampling Compresses the TF--AR Gap}\label{subsec:ss}
